candidates.review: Came back flapping, not soaring: the wings raised high in a deep V on the upstroke, the body nearly upright like a perched pigeon with a plump breast, the legs and talons dangling forward, the tail hanging at about 60 degrees. The head is small-billed (a thin short hook, not the massive eagle bill). The body would need a 45 degree pitch that points the head down, a re-bent neck, the legs removed and a new tail, so the red-tail's level flight body (already long-headed with a big hooked bill) was used instead and the wings rebuilt from our own outline.

accuracy_notes: Reads as an adult bald eagle at every tier: from below and above a dark chocolate plank-winged raptor with a white head and big yellow bill projecting well ahead and a white wedge tail; seven well-separated fingers; flat-winged (2 degrees), so it does not read as a vulture or harrier when it banks. The underwing is dark with a slightly paler grey-brown band on the flight-feather bases and a dark trailing edge. Still open: the body is the red-tail's (scaled 1.4x and reshaped), so the head and neck are a little slim for an eagle and the bill, though deepened, is the hawk's hook; the white hood ends in a ragged line where the body faces meet; the eye is a small pale-yellow octahedron (lod0 only); no feet or legs (deleted, as the hawk's); the tail is a smooth plate with no feather separation; no juvenile or subadult plumage (mottled brown and white), which is common on the Olympic Peninsula's rivers in winter; no perched model (the eagle on a snag over the Hoh would need one). A local birder should check the wing breadth and the head projection against soaring Hoh River eagles.
